Section Forty-Two, Part One: Explaining the Title of the Sūtra.
Question:
The titles of various sūtras are established either by way of person, dharma, cause, or fruit; their essential forms are manifold. I do not yet understand from what basis this sūtra derives its name.
I look up to you to analyze and elucidate this title.
I reply:

I have heard that the ultimate truth is wordless, yet it cannot be revealed without words; one who wishes to exhaustively fathom the wondrous principle must rely upon the "trap" (the means), and thus names are provisionally established within the nameless.
“Mahāvaipulya” (Great and Vast) refers to the Dharma realized;
“Buddhāvataṃsaka” (Flower Ornament of the Buddha) refers to the person who realizes it.

“Great” signifies that its essential nature is all-encompassing; “vast” signifies that its functional activity is universal. “Buddha” means the fruition is perfected and awakening is fulfilled; “flower” is a metaphor for the blossoming of the myriad practices; “ornament” means adorning the Dharma to perfect the person; and “sūtra” means threading together the eternal Dharma.

The essence and function of the entire scripture are fully encompassed by "Mahāvaipulya" (Great Vaipulya), while the five cycles of cause and effect are all "Buddhāvataṃsaka" (Flower Ornament of the Buddha).

This constitutes a dual title of person and dharma, wherein both the dharma and its metaphor are presented together; it possesses both essence and function, as well as fruit and cause. Its principles are exhaustive and its meanings perfect, subsuming everything without exception. It encompasses inconceivable doctrines as the grand framework of this entire work; yet, were I to explain them in full detail, I fear it would weary both your sight and hearing.
I respectfully respond.
Second, clarifying the essential tenets of the Sūtras.
Question:
Now, every statement must have its foundation, and every principle must have its ultimate destination.
I do not yet know: what dharma-gate does this sutra take as its primary tenet, and toward what direction does its underlying intent incline?
I shall respond in full to show you where it leads, so that within these concise words you may perceive its profound essence.
Response:
When the collar is raised and the main thread is pulled, the individual hairs and eyes naturally fall into order.
By tracing back to the root and attaining the source, the branches and currents naturally become clear.

This is the "patriarchal school of no-patriarch," wherein both the doctrine and its exposition are fully elucidated; this sutra takes as its central tenet the inconceivable causality of the true principle of the dharmadhātu-dependent origination.

The Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is the general characteristic; it encompasses both phenomena and principle, as well as that which is unobstructed, serving as a standard and support for all, and is fully present within the constituent nature.
Dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) refers to the great function of this essence.
"Principle in reality" (*lishi*) refers specifically to the principle;
"cause and effect" (*yin-guo*) specifically clarifies the phenomena.

This sutra’s central tenet elucidates the cultivation of the perfect cause through six stages and the realization of the full fruit of the ten bodies; each and every one accords with "principle in reality," as they are all the great gateway of the dharma-realm dependent origination.
In terms of the ultimate principle, reality is tranquil, vast, and empty; thus the Sūtra says:

"The nature of phenomena is fundamentally quiescent and devoid of all marks, like space it is non-discriminative; transcending all grasping and attachment, it is beyond the path of words—truly equal and eternally pure."
When one speaks of dependent origination, myriad virtues unfold in profusion; thus the Sūtra says: "Within the foremost ultimate reality, he manifests various types of conventional activities."
Because these two are unimpeded, phenomena and principle penetrate one another, mutually subsuming each other until both vanish.

When these two are mutually perfected, phenomena and principle illuminate and adhere to one another; when principle is made real to harmonize cause and effect, they enter into one another in infinite layers. When these two are unified and returned to the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), they are profoundly interpenetrating and harmonious. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Within the realm of the conditioned (saṃskṛta-dhātu), one demonstrates the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta-dharma), yet without destroying the characteristics of the conditioned;
within the realm of the unconditioned, one demonstrates the conditioned, yet without discriminating the nature of the unconditioned."
"By virtue of this mastery, there is nothing that is not penetrated; yet because it is realized through direct correspondence (*yoga*), it transcends words and thought.

Encompassing all without exception, this is the core tenet of the sutra. Regarding its underlying intent, by contemplating it, one achieves meditative observation and swiftly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood."
I respectfully respond.
Third, explaining the name of the Buddha.
Question:
In various sūtras and śāstras, it is frequently stated that Śākyamuni or Vairocana are distinct designations for the three bodies (trikāya).
By what principle does this sūtra identify this very Śākyamuni as being named Vairocana?
Question: Why are the names of Śakra and Brahmā used together in the invocation?
Answer:

Generally, teachings vary according to the capacities of sentient beings, and there are many paths regarding the provisional and the ultimate. The classification of the three bodies (trikāya) as distinct designations belongs specifically to the teachings within the Three Vehicles.

Now, the profound purport of the One Vehicle is such that its single essence is undivided: the provisional designation of Śākyamuni is precisely the real, and the reality of Vairocana is precisely the provisional.
Thus, the Sūtra says, "He is sometimes named Vairocana, and sometimes named Śākyamuni"; the names are non-dual.
Śākyamuni: Śākya means "Able One" (Capable One);
Muni means "Silent Sage. Vairocana:
This means "Universal Radiance" (Light Shining Everywhere).

The two lights of body and wisdom illuminate both phenomena and principle simultaneously; perfectly bright and uniquely luminous, their names are established as provisional designations. In reality, within this single Sahā world there are ten trillion such names, and throughout the entire Dharma-realm, these names are inexhaustible. These names are employed according to what is appropriate to gather sentient beings, whether one or many, depending on the capacity of the recipient; they are merely provisional names used to manifest inexhaustible virtues.
I respectfully respond.
Fourth, the Dharma intent regarding participation in assemblies.
Question:
To inspire faith in sentient beings, one must speak of time, place, and person; although the Dharmakāya is all-pervasive, its teaching necessarily has a specific location.
It is not yet known at what time this sutra was spoken, nor in how many assemblies it was taught.
Was this spoken by the Buddha alone,
or was it entrusted to another?
I respond to these matters with due respect so that there may be no confusion.
Answer:

The Dharma-body is neither localized nor non-localized; yet, as the function of its very essence, its manifestations must necessarily have specific locations. Briefly stated, there are seven distinct locations, though in reality, these locations exhaust the entire Dharma-realm.
Regarding the "seven locations": the first assembly was at the Bodhimaṇḍa;

the second assembly was at the Hall of Universal Radiance (Vairocanavyūha-maṇḍala); the third assembly was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the fourth assembly was in the Yāma Heaven; the fifth assembly was in the Tuṣita Heaven; the sixth assembly was in the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven; and the seventh assembly was in the Jeta Grove.
Furthermore, because the three assemblies are universally radiant, there are nine assemblies in total:
the first assembly was held at the Bodhimaṇḍa to expound the causes and effects of the Tathāgata’s dependent retribution;
the second assembly was held in the Hall of Universal Radiance to expound the Dharma-gate of the Ten Faiths.
In the third assembly, at the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he taught the Dharma of the Ten Abodes;
in the fourth assembly, at the palace of the Yāma Heaven, he taught the Dharma of the Ten Practices;
and in the fifth assembly, at Tuṣita Heaven, he taught the Dharma of the Ten Transferences.

In the sixth assembly, at the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*), he expounded the Dharma of the Ten Stages (*Daśabhūmi*); because there is a distinction between the noble ones (*ārya*) and the ordinary, this assembly bypasses the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*).

In the seventh assembly, in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsadharmasabhā*), he expounded the Dharma of the fulfillment of causes and the perfection of fruits; it consists of eleven chapters of sutra: the first six concern the fulfillment of causes, and the latter five concern the perfection of fruits.
In the eighth assembly, in the Hall of Universal Radiance, he expounded the Dharma of the Great Practices of Samantabhadra, wherein the six stages are realized instantaneously.

In the ninth assembly, at the Jeta Grove in Śrāvastī, he preached the Dharma-gate of Entering the Dharma-realm; yet, as the ninth assembly concludes with his return to the Bodhimaṇḍa, the tenth assembly reaches its perfect clarity, suddenly manifesting the ultimate mystery.

Regarding whether these words were spoken by the Buddha alone or entrusted to others: this sutra intends to demonstrate that all Buddhas speak in unison; thus, in most assemblies, it is the Buddhas of the ten directions who empower Bodhisattvas to speak, intending to clarify that what one speaks, all speak.

In the first assembly, all the Buddhas of the ten directions empower Samantabhadra Bodhisattva to preach; this is because Samantabhadra is the presiding lord of the ocean-like assembly of the *Avataṃsaka* and represents the Universal Dharma (*samantadharma*).

In the second assembly, Mañjuśrī is the presiding lord and the ten-headed [Bodhisattvas] discourse together; this represents that the gate of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) is the foremost of the myriad virtues.
The third assembly was taught by the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, signifying that the mind of Dharma-wisdom increases through the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
The fourth assembly was taught by the Bodhisattva Guṇakara-vana, signifying that the forest of practices of the Dharma-gates of the ten practices (*caryā*) stands tall and dense.
The fifth assembly was spoken by Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva, signifying the meaning of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) as being loftily directed toward the ultimate.
The sixth assembly was spoken by Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, signifying that the dharmas of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) contain and give rise to that which is indestructible.

The seventh assembly was also spoken by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, signifying that the causes are perfected and the fruits are fulfilled, such that the practices and virtues universally pervade the entire Dharma-realm.

The eighth assembly was also spoken by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; it subsumes the names of the six stages and condenses the practices of the six stages into two thousand modes of practice. By citing one to encompass the whole, it shows that from the initial aspiration until the ultimate stage of Equal Enlightenment, all cultivate these together, not abandoning the causal practices even upon attaining Buddhahood.

In the ninth assembly, the Tathāgata himself enters the Lion’s Stretching Samādhi and causes the great multitude to suddenly realize the Dharma-realm by manifesting signs and preaching; this is further developed by the two sages Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī, and all the spiritual friends of the hundred cities likewise speak in concert. Therefore, this single assembly is divided into two parts:
first, the primary assembly where the Tathāgata manifests signs and the two sages reveal and clarify the sudden realization of the Dharma-realm;

second, from the end of the sixty-first scripture through the conclusion of the eightieth, the various spiritual friends preach for Sudhana, clarifying the gradual realization of the Dharma-realm, wherein the gradual and the sudden are interwoven and the root and the branches mutually reflect one another, as all realize the Dharma-realm.
A brief clarification of the locations where the assemblies gather is as follows according to the manifest text.
If one were to extract the passages from the sūtra individually, there are ten locations in total:

first, this Jambudvīpa; second, throughout a hundred billion worlds; third, pervading the ten directions; fourth, reaching the end of all atoms; fifth, penetrating other realms; sixth, encompassing the dust-motes of lands; seventh, repeatedly gathering lands; eighth, again gathering them in layers; ninth, like a net of Indra; and tenth, the same for all Buddhas.

Thus, summarizing the general assembly, the speakers are as infinite as the motes of dust in the three thousandfold world-system and pervade the entire dharma-realm; there is nothing among the three types of worlds that they do not expound.
These nine assemblies are condensed into four divisions:

the first assembly, from the "Chapter on the Sublime Adornment of the World-Ruling Lords" to the "Chapter on Vairocana," consists of eleven fascicles of scripture and is titled the "Division Exhorting Joyful Faith by Illustrating the Fruit."

The second section consists of thirty-one chapters and forty-one fascicles of scripture, spanning from the "Chapter on the Names of the Tathāgatas" to the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" in the second assembly; it is titled the "Section on Cultivating Causes and Corresponding to the Fruit to Generate Understanding."

The third [division] consists of seven fascicles of scripture from the single chapter "Leaving the World" (*Lokottara*) of the eighth assembly, titled "The Section on Entrusting the Dharma to Advance in Practice and Accomplish Conduct.

The fourth consists of twenty-one fascicles of scripture from the single chapter "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Dharmadhātupraveśa*) of the ninth assembly, titled "The Section on Relying on Persons to Realize Entry and Accomplish Virtue."
If the nine assemblies are expanded into thirty-nine chapters, the first assembly consists of six chapters:

first, "The Exquisite Adornment of the World Rulers"; second, "The Manifestation of Signs by the Tathāgata"; third, "Samādhi of Samantabhadra"; fourth, "The Formation of the World"; fifth, "The Flower Treasury World"; and sixth, "Vairocana."
The second assembly also consists of six chapters:

first, the "Chapter on the Names and Epithets of the Tathāgata"; second, the "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths"; third, the "Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance"; fourth, the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Clarity"; fifth, the "Chapter on Pure Conduct"; and sixth, the "Chapter on the Worthy Head."
The third assembly also consists of six chapters:

first, "Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven Palace"; second, "Verses of Praise in the Trāyastriṃśa Palace"; third, "The Ten Stages"; fourth, "Brahmacarya"; fifth, "The Merit of First Resolving for Enlightenment"; and sixth, "Clarifying the Dharma."
The fourth assembly consists of four chapters:
first, "Ascending to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven"; second, "Verses of Praise within the Palace of the Yāma Heaven"; third, "The Ten Practices"; and fourth, "The Ten Stores."
The fifth assembly consists of three chapters:
first, "Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace"; second, "Verses of Praise within the Tuṣita Palace"; and third, "The Ten Dedications."
The first chapter of the sixth assembly:
"The Ten Stages" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*).
The seventh assembly contains eleven chapters:

1. "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis," 2. "Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers," 3. "Chapter on the Ten Endurances," 4. "Chapter on the Incalculable," 5. "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata," and 6. "Chapter on the Abodes of Bodhisattvas"—these six clarify the perfection of the causes for equal enlightenment. 7. "Chapter on the Inconceivable Dharmas of the Buddha," 8. "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata," 9. "Chapter on the Merits of the Minor Marks and Radiance," 10. "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra," and 11. "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata."
The eighth assembly consists of a single chapter, namely the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (Lokottara-parivarta).
The ninth assembly also consists of a single chapter, namely the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma Realm" (Dharmadhātu-praveśa-parivarta).

The first three assemblies each contain six chapters, totaling eighteen chapters; the fourth and fifth assemblies together have seven chapters, making twenty-five chapters; the seventh assembly has eleven chapters, thus reaching thirty-six chapters; and since the sixth, eighth, ninth, and third assemblies each have only one chapter, there are thirty-nine chapters in total.
Furthermore, the thirty-nine chapters are grouped into three divisions:

first, the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World-Ruling Lord" (*Lokendrarājavyūha*) constitutes the introductory section (*nidāna*); second, from the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" (*Prādurbhāva-lakṣaṇa*) onwards constitutes the main body (*śarīra*); and third, from the sixty-first sūtra of the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Gandavyūha*), beginning with "At that time, Mañjuśrī emerged from the Good Abiding Pavilion" (*atha khalu mañjuśrīḥ kumārabhūtaḥ suvihāra-kūṭāgārān niṣkramya*), until the end of the scripture, constitutes the dissemination section (*pariṇāmana*).
The thirty-nine chapters harmonize the True Doctrine, while the nine assemblies and four divisions manifest its grand structure.
Although the extant text appears thus, the complete original is difficult to manifest; only by examining its titles can one come to know its essential framework.
I respectfully respond.
Fifth, not arising to ascend to heaven.
Question:
Since their going and staying differ and their realms—human and celestial—are distinct, how can the Sūtra state that [the Buddha] ascended to the three heavens without rising from the Bodhi tree?

Furthermore, if one grants that he ascended without rising, this principle should apply equally to all; why then is this statement made specifically regarding the assembly of the Three Worthies (trayaḥ-ārya-pudgalāḥ)?
Therefore, the "Chapter on Ascending to the Palace in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven" states:

"At that time, the Tathāgata, without leaving the foot of the Bodhi tree, ascended to the palace of Śakra on the summit of Mount Sumeru; he ascended to the Yāma heaven for the second time and the Tuṣita heaven for the third. Why is it that these specific words are mentioned only here?
Answer: The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is vast and empty; dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is inconceivable.

Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, takes the Dharma-realm as his body and unifies dependent origination as his function. Body and function are without obstruction, and unity and multiplicity are sovereign. He is pervasive without being divided and omnipresent without moving. He responds to stimuli and brings all things into communication, yet those who perceive him appear to do so sequentially.

Those in Jambudvīpa who have a karmic affinity perceive the Buddha within Jambudvīpa; those in the celestial palaces who have a karmic affinity perceive him ascending to heaven. It is not that the Buddha, who is the Awakened Tree itself, is moved from here to ascend to that heaven.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati said:
"O Son of the Buddha, you should observe the Tathāgata’s power of mastery: throughout all of Jambudvīpa, everyone says the Buddha is therein."
"We now see the Buddha dwelling upon the summit of Mount Sumeru; so it is throughout the ten directions—such is the sovereign power of the Tathāgata.
This clearly demonstrates that both going and staying are merely perceptions of the phenomenal world.
Please illustrate this with a metaphor.
It is like a single moon reflected in a clear river, observed by three boats;
one boat remains stationary while the other two move south and north.

Those facing south see the moon and follow it for a thousand li to the south; those facing north see the moon and follow it for a thousand li to the north; while those whose boat has come to rest see the moon as unmoving. Thus, this moon does not leave the middle of the stream to travel toward the south or the north.

Suppose a hundred thousand people were to observe together; as they each move away from the eight directions, a hundred thousand moons would likewise recede, such that their departure and staying appear distinct.
Those who possess wisdom understand this profound principle for themselves.

He asked again: "In principle, what precedes and what follows should be aligned; why is it that only these three stages of the Sages (trīṇi kṣānti-kṣaṇāni) possess this specific intent? [The answer is: It is to manifest a distinction in meaning.

That is to say, because the first two assemblies are adjacent to one another, they do not require the inclusion of what precedes; whereas these three involve a separation by humans and devas, and thus must be connected by including what precedes.

Furthermore, these three assemblies equally elucidate the stage of the Sage (*bhadra*). In the sixth assembly, those who have already realized and entered [the path] do not require the preceding stages; in the seventh, the stage of Samantabhadra within the bodhisattva stages and the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣmabodhi*) naturally do not require them; in the eighth, the essence and function of the six stages are suddenly revealed as already integrated; and in the ninth, it clarifies only that the realization of their essence and function is of a single flavor. Therefore, in all these cases, they do not require [the preceding stages].
It is solely because the three assemblies are intended to be formed into a single dharma-realm through a linked chain.
This is my respectful response.
Sixth, the timing of the preaching of the sutra.
Question:

The Tathāgata appeared in the world some fifty years ago; throughout his single period of transformation, there were differences regarding three or five periods. I do not know at what time this sutra was preached.
When you respectfully recount these matters to dispel doubts and obstructions, I reply:

When the mind merges with the Ultimate Way, it becomes one with both past and present; within the Dharma-realm there is no arising, and from the beginning, temporal divisions are absent. How much more so when infinite discourse reveals that kalpas and thoughts are perfectly interfused—indeed, at the moment of the initial attainment of Perfect Enlightenment, the perfect and subtle nature is instantaneously manifested.
From the narrow to the broad, there are roughly ten levels of distinction: first, a single thought-moment; second, the full seven days;

third, pervading the three periods of time; fourth, encompassing kalpas of the same category; fifth, gathering kalpas of different categories; sixth, subsuming kalpas within a thought-moment; seventh, the mutual inclusion of kalpas and thought-moments; eighth, the time of realms of different categories; ninth, the mutual penetration of this and that; and tenth, subsuming the derivative within the fundamental, whereby what is not a kalpa becomes a kalpa.
Briefly outlining the ten layers, each one encompasses the whole; it is neither long nor short, yet capable of being both long and short.
This is my respectful response.
Seventh: Regarding the categories of the sutras, the question is:
The expositions of the Noble Teachings vary in their breadth and brevity;
it is not yet known whether this teaching is extensive, concise, complete, or incomplete.
Answer:
The wordless word exhausts the Dharma-realm;
the unspeakable teaching leaves no phenomenon unexplained.
Briefly, based on verbal explanation, ten layers of distinctions are established:

The first is the abbreviated version of the sutra, which is the eighty-fascicle text currently transmitted in thirty-nine chapters; this is because its original Sanskrit manuscript contained one hundred thousand verses, whereas the current translation comprises only forty-five thousand.

Second is the "abbreviated version" (xiàběn) of the sutra, which consists of one hundred thousand verses in forty-eight chapters; this is the version that the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna beheld in the Dragon Palace, as there were three versions in total, and this is the abbreviated one.
The *Mūlasūtra* among the three versions consists of four hundred and ninety-eight thousand eight hundred verses and one thousand two hundred chapters, as seen by him.

The *Uttarasūtra* among the four versions was also seen by him; it contains as many verses as there are atoms in thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms and as many chapters as there are atoms in a single four-continent world system (*cāturdvīpaka*).
Among these, the latter two texts are not capable of being transmitted by the mental power of ordinary people.

As for the fifth, the *Universal Eye Sūtra*, it was held by the third spiritual friend, Samudramegha, whom Sudhana saw. Even with ink equal in volume to the great ocean and pens as numerous as the Mount Sumerus, one could not write even a small fraction of this Universal Eye Dharma-gate—let alone its entirety—considering that within a single chapter there is a single gate, within a single gate a single dharma, within a single dharma a single meaning, and within a single meaning a single phrase. How much less could one exhaust it all!
Because only Bodhisattvas who possess total retention (*dhāraṇī*) are able to receive and uphold it.

Sixth is the commonality of preaching the sūtras: that within a single category of world-systems—extending throughout the dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, even in a space the size of a hair-tip—one speaks with vocal sound without end.

Seventh are the scriptures of divergent teachings; that is to say, since the lands and worlds—such as those shaped like trees and so forth—are diverse, their conventional designations are also distinct. It is impossible to definitively determine whether they are of a certain form or language, as their categories are difficult to standardize.
Regarding the Sūtra on the Eight Lords and Retinues: if Vairocana Buddha is the principal, then the Buddhas of the ten directions are his retinue;
if the Buddhas of the ten directions are the principals, then Vairocana and all others are their retinue. Thus it is.

The *Navaparivāra-sūtra* (Nine Retinue Sūtras) refers to those other teachings for which [certain beings] are not suitable vessels and thus do not hear this universally applicable discourse; since all teachings spoken according to what is appropriate enter this gateway, they are called "Retinue Sūtras."

The *Sūtra on the Ten Perfections* refers to the total integration of the aforementioned versions into a single, inexhaustible ocean of teaching; thus, not a single word or phrase is left unencompassed.

Because that which is expressed (the meaning) is inconceivable, the means of expression (the words) are difficult to illustrate. Briefly, ten categories are set forth to demonstrate this profound gateway; yet even these abbreviated explanations encompass the full range of principles, for they share the same moist nature as a drop of water from the ocean.
I respectfully respond.
Eighth, the Translation and Transmission.
Question:

Now, the teaching has flowed from the Western Heaven to the Eastern lands of China; the *pātra* Sanskrit scripts have been transcribed and transmitted onto paper. This must surely rely upon the grace of a brilliant imperial decree and depend upon the detailed deliberations of the multitude of worthies.
It is not yet known in which dynasty this scripture was translated,
nor who its translator was.
As there are similarities and differences between the new and old versions, I respectfully submit this inquiry to clarify their essential meaning and enable one to recognize their vast source.
Answer:
Since the sun of the Buddha set its radiance and the compilation took place in the Western Heaven, the teachings first reached the eastern lands during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han.
This inconceivable sutra appeared only during the Jin dynasty; it has been transmitted in four different versions with variations in both content and sequence.

In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra from Northern India—whose name means "Awakened Virtue" (Jue Xian) in the language of Tang—translated thirty-six thousand verses from the Sanskrit original into sixty fascicles of the Jin scriptures at Xiesikong Temple (the present-day Shanggang Xingyan Temple) in Yangzhou.
The śramaṇa Faye transcribed the text, while Huayan and Huiguan polished it.

In the first year of the Yonglong era of the second Great Tang (680 CE), the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānabhadra from Central India—whose name means "Sunshine" in Chinese—at Tayuan Temple in the Western Capital (the present-day Chongfu Temple in Chang’an), translated the "Entering the Dharma Realm Chapter."
Two passages have been omitted from within:
first, the section from after Lady Māyā up to before Bodhisattva Maitreya, which includes the ten spiritual friends such as Devendra-prabha and others.

Ninth, the essence and characteristics of the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*).
Question:
The Flower Treasury Ocean of Lands is that which is brought forth through the cultivation of the pure land contemplation based on the *sāmbhogika* (enjoyment) support of the Tathāgata.
I do not yet know what kind of physical form is established therein, nor can I hear of its adornments or its transformative teachings.
By cultivating what causes is this ocean of lands accomplished?
What practices and deeds are established so as to roam within it?
Please show us the entrance by which we may know where to turn for refuge.
Answer:
My Buddha-land is the perfect fusion of the environment and its inhabitants; its essence is True Suchness (Tathatā), and its magnitude pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
As for its adornments, they equal the atoms within all lands; its Dharma-transformations extend horizontally and exhaustively vertically throughout the boundless.
The cultivation of the cause is so remote that its calculation is difficult to measure; only through the perfect cultivation of a perfect capacity can one realize this realm.

Nevertheless, according to the capacities of beings, it appears or remains hidden, pure or impure, deficient or full, manifesting in varying degrees of shallowness and depth, and as both small and great.
Although it undergoes waxing and waning, the pure and the defiled interpenetrate; although it appears as large or small, the pervasive and the localized are mutually fused.
Its consciousness and wisdom are immeasurable, so how could words ever exhaustively describe them?
Therefore, relying on the scriptures, I shall briefly indicate their characteristics.

This Flower Treasury World consists of twenty tiers; as for the distance from the very bottom tier to the second tier, it is reached only after passing through as many worlds as there are atoms in a single Buddha-field.
From the second up to the third, fourth, and so on, through the twentieth layer, the numbers of distant and near [worlds] gradually increase accordingly.
This Sahā world is the thirteenth layer.

At the very bottom of the Flower Adornment Treasury, first spread wind-circles as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru; upon these wind-circles is supported the fragrant water-ocean of Universal Radiance Mani-jewels, from which emerges a lotus named Various Radiant Pistil-Fragrance Banner.

In the Flower-Holding Ocean of Realms, within the fragrant flowers of its filaments there are lotus pedestals; atop these pedestals are diamond-rimmed mountains that encircle them in every direction. Within this enclosure lies the great earth, level and even on all four sides, pure, firm, and solid.

Within these, there are fragrant water seas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields; each sea is of a single type, and within each type there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields. Between each of these seas, there are fragrant water rivers as numerous as the atoms in four continents, spiraling to the right in encircling succession.

However, its ground-substance is diamond, adorned with a multitude of various exquisite jewels; every single realm is further embellished by pure merits as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of worlds.

The Sūtra says: "Within every single atom of all the worlds of Flower Treasury, one perceives the entire Dharma-realm; the radiance of jewels manifests Buddhas gathering like clouds—this is the Tathāgata’s mastery over his buddha-field."

"All of this was brought forth by the Great Practices cultivated by our World-Honored One over many kalpas in the past; therefore, the Sūtra says: 'Because the World-Honored One cultivated meritorious and pure deeds in the presence of as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust throughout all realms of existence, he has obtained this ocean of world-systems adorned with various jewel-light flower-treasuries.'"
It is further stated: "The Flower Treasury World-Ocean is undifferentiated from the Dharma-realm; its adornments are entirely pure, abiding within empty space.

Thus we know that although there are inexhaustible adornments, each one accords with the Dharma-realm. If one’s contemplation is perfected, one will be born therein; there is no cause among the ten thousand practices that does not lead toward it.

However, as for its general meaning, whether in terms of retribution or response, there is no obstruction whatsoever. To briefly set forth ten aspects to manifest this inconceivability: first, the non-obstruction of phenomena and principle; second, the non-obstruction of formation and disintegration;

third, the non-obstruction of the vast and the narrow; fourth, the non-obstruction of mutual interpenetration; fifth, the non-obstruction of mutual identity; sixth, the non-obstruction of the minute; seventh, the non-obstruction of concealment and manifestation; eighth, the non-obstruction of repeated appearance; ninth, the non-obstruction of principal and attendant; and tenth, the non-obstruction of time and place.
To accord with one unimpededness is to possess all unimpededness; when contemplation is perfected, it naturally proceeds of its own accord.
This is my respectful reply.
Tenth: The Mutual Penetration of Sentient Beings and Buddhas.
Question:
Sentient beings and Buddhas differ in their states of delusion and awakening; sentient beings circulate through the six realms of existence, while Buddhas are perfected with myriad virtues.
How can it be said that "sentient beings are themselves Buddhas," such that these two states mutually encompass one another?
To confuse cause and effect is entirely contrary to the principles of the Dharma.
Answer:
Now, the true source is non-dual and its wondrous intent is ever uniform; it is only because of differences in delusion and awakening that there arise the categories of sentient beings and Buddhas.
Deluded regarding the truth, one gives rise to delusion and is provisionally termed a "sentient being"; realizing that the substance of delusion is itself the truth, one is called a "Buddha.
When deluded, one is entirely deluded regarding the truth, for there is no delusion apart from the truth;
when awakened, the essence of delusion is fundamentally the truth, and it is not something newly produced.
The cause of delusion, ignorance, arises adventitiously, like mistakenly taking east for west;
awakening is said to arise from accord with ultimate truth, like the fact that east is inherently unchanging.

In terms of appearances, one conventionally speaks of "birth" and "Buddhahood," yet from the perspective of essence, these aspects can be mutually subsumed. Failing to perceive this source, one remains deluded and does not awaken; by comprehending this profound mystery, one attains Buddhahood in an instant.

The Sūtra says: "The realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) are ultimately without distinction; to know them all completely is the sphere of the Tathāgata.
As soon as the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he universally perceives that all sentient beings have already attained perfect enlightenment;
yet while sentient beings remain in delusion, they undergo suffering within the heart of the Buddha.
I hope that those who aspire to the profound mystery will not abandon the delusive in their quest for the true.
This is my respectful response.
Number Eleven: The Perfect Subtlety of the Ten Faiths.
Question:

The ten stages of faith constitute the beginning, and the perfection of wisdom constitutes the end. Although a tree that fills one's arms originates from a tiny hair-tip, the hair-tip itself cannot yet reach the clouds;
likewise, although wondrous enlightenment is accomplished through faith, how can mere faith encompass such a station?
Now you say that within the stage of faith, the perfect and wondrous is suddenly revealed.
Although I have heard these words, I do not yet understand their meaning.
I respectfully submit this inquiry in order to dispel my doubts.
Answer:

Teachings have their degrees of depth, and faculties have their variations of superiority and inferiority. From the subtle to the manifest, the gradual teaching is used to guide those of inferior capacity;
the initial mind is suddenly perfected, as the perfect teaching is intended for those of superior caliber.
Having perfected faith and perfected understanding, one cultivates the myriad practices in their entirety; through sudden awakening and sudden realization, the myriad virtues are fully perfected.

It would be like becoming a lady of Yue in the morning and a consort of Wu in the evening, or being born in a royal palace at dusk and being hailed as a crown prince at dawn—how could one require a gradual progression through stages before becoming a sovereign?
I respectfully respond.
Twelfth, the differences between the obstacles of delusion.
Question:

The two obstacles are more numerous than the sands of the Ganges and cannot even be compared [to them]; they have not yet attained the name of "severed" even after incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*). Since the noble ones of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) eliminate them gradually and partially, how could there be a severance of all at once?
Since this transcends conventional norms, it is difficult to inspire confidence.
Answer:
Delusion originally has no source, yet it suddenly arises from the obscuration of the Truth; being deluded and failing to return, it spreads boundlessly and without limit.
If a slender cloud brushes across the sky, its arrival comes from nowhere; in an instant, it fills the six directions with a profound darkness.
When a long wind suddenly arises, the clouds vanish in a flash; for a thousand li there is not a single speck, and the myriad phenomena appear with vivid clarity.
The winds of skillful means arise to illuminate that delusion has no root; the emptiness of nature manifests, and the foundation of all virtues becomes perfect.
The eighty thousand afflictions are all *pāramitās*; the sands-of-the-Ganges of delusive obstructions are all gates of truth.
As long as the cataracts of the eyes have not been removed, illusory flowers will continue to proliferate in confusion; yet once the Dharma-eye is purified, what delusion would not be dispelled?
How could such stubborn attachment persist for so many kalpas?
I respectfully respond.

Thirteenth: The Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata. Question: The sūtras and śāstras commonly state that the Buddha has three bodies; whether they are expanded, they do not go beyond the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the distinction between self and others, or whether they are condensed, they merely divide them into the True Body (*dharmakāya*) and the Responsive Body (*nirmāṇakāya*). How is it that there are ten? Answer: The three bodies are established based on the principle of the One Mind. Because the essence of this mind is intrinsically pure, it is called the *svābhāvikakāya* (Self-Nature Body). Because its nature is luminous and unobstructed, it is called the *dharmakāya* (Dharma Body). Because its function is all-pervasive and unimpeded, it is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body). Because its manifestations are diverse and inexhaustible, it is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (Responsive Body). These four bodies encompass all dharmas and are not separate from one another. Furthermore, because the essence of the Dharma Body is eternally quiescent and free from outflows, it is called the *tathatākāya* (Suchness Body). Because the nature of the Dharma Body is originally non-arising and non-ceasing, it is called the *anutpādadharmakāya* (Non-Arising Dharma Body). Because the function of the Dharma Body is universally pervasive and unobstructed, it is called the *jñānakāya* (Wisdom Body). Because the manifestations of the Dharma Body are infinite and inexhaustible, it is called the *anantajñānakāya* (Infinite Wisdom Body). Moreover, because the essence of the Enjoyment Body is pure and serene, it is called the *sukhakāya* (Bliss Body). Because the nature of the Enjoyment Body is majestic and dignified, it is called the *vibhūṣaṇakāya* (Adornment Body). Because the function of the Enjoyment Body is subtle and wondrous, it is called the *lakṣaṇakāya* (Characteristic Body). Because the manifestations of the Enjoyment Body are vast and boundless, it is called the *anantavyūhakāya* (Infinite Array Body).

Furthermore, because the essence of the Responsive Body is skillful and expedient, it is called the *upāyakāya* (Expedient Means Body). Because the nature of the Responsive Body is versatile and adaptable, it is called the *vaśitākāya* (Mastery Body). Because the function of the Responsive Body is inconceivable, it is called the *acintyakāya* (Inconceivable Body). Because the manifestations of the Responsive Body are immeasurable, it is called the *apramāṇakāya* (Immeasurable Body). Thus, these ten bodies are each distinct yet mutually inclusive. This is why the sūtras and śāstras speak of three bodies, while other teachings speak of four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten bodies. All of these are established based on the principle of the One Mind. Therefore, although the names differ, their substance is identical. It is only because sentient beings have various capacities for understanding that the teachings are presented differently. This is why the sūtras and śāstras sometimes speak of three bodies and sometimes of ten. This concludes the section on the Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata. Based on what reasoning are the ten bodies thus taught?
Please provide their ten names and indicate their essential natures and characteristics.
Answer:
The True Body (*dharmakāya*) is vast and profound, its essence unified with the *dharmadhātu*; it encompasses all without exterior, its function equaling that of the myriad transformations.

When tracing back to the source, there is no duality; yet when grasping at traces, there are many aspects. The Buddhas, according to the capacities of sentient beings, provide diverse explanations regarding the one and the many; summarizing these in terms of essence, characteristics, and function, they briefly speak of the three bodies (*trikāya*).

Generally speaking, with respect to both self and others, there are two categories: the enjoyment bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the true-response bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). Explaining this according to the ultimate principle, the ten bodies (*daśakāya*) are fully encompassed.
Regarding these ten bodies, there are briefly two types:
first, the integration of the three worlds to constitute the ten bodies; [the second being the classification of the ten bodies based on their distinct characteristics].

Second, a single body of a Tathāgata inherently possesses ten bodies, namely: first, the body of enlightenment (*bodhi-kāya*); second, the body of vows (*praṇidhāna-kāya*); third, the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*); fourth, the sustaining body (*baladhara-kāya*); fifth, the body adorned with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana-saṃskṛta-kāya*); sixth, the body of majestic power (*anubhāva-kāya*); seventh, the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*); eighth, the body of merit (*puṇya-kāya*); ninth, the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*); and tenth, the wisdom-body (*jñāna-kāya*).

However, these ten bodies are precisely the ten virtues of the Buddha; they possess both substance and function, and include both the responsive (nirmāṇakāya) and the true (dharmakāya). Yet, because they are fused within the gate of non-duality, they are termed "perfect and wondrous.
What are these ten virtues?

First, awakening at the tree of enlightenment, attaining great and clear realization; second, fulfilling vows throughout the Dharma-realm by ascending to Tuṣita Heaven; third, manifesting transformations in manifold ways, like the moon dividing into many reflections in water; fourth, sustaining power for eternity through both the whole-body and fragmentary-body relics; fifth, possessing boundless marks and signs, as numerous as the atoms of dust; sixth, majestic authority that outshines all else, like the moon eclipsing the stars; seventh, responding to requests with unimpeded penetration, as swift as one’s wishes; eighth, profound merit and virtue, like the ocean containing all things; ninth, the true permanence of the Dharma-nature, serene and all-pervasive; tenth, decisive wisdom, suddenly awakened and perfectly luminous.
The ten virtues do not depart from a single body; there is no separate Buddha apart from them. This is unlike the three bodies or four wisdoms, where essence and function are distinct.
Regarding the statement that these ten bodies are fused with the three worlds:

first, the sentient-being body; second, the land-body; third, the karmic-retribution body; fourth, the śrāvaka body; fifth, the pratyekabuddha body; sixth, the bodhisattva body; seventh, the Tathāgata body; eighth, the wisdom-body; ninth, the dharma-body; and tenth, the space-body.

Since a single Tathāgata-body already possesses ten bodies, the same applies to the remaining nine bodies, thereby forming one hundred bodies; furthermore, as they mutually interpenetrate, they form one thousand bodies.
Thus, the true and the responsive are fused, and unity and multiplicity are sovereign; it is hoped that you will look up to this with faith, remain unhindered, and hear this constantly.
I respectfully respond.
Fourteenth: The Ranks of the Sages and Worthies.
Question:
The sūtras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna establish successive stages; it is not yet known how the stages of this teaching are arranged.
Answer:
In principle there is no difference in depth, but in realization there are gradations.

Because the noble ones differ in their realization of unconditioned dharmas—some having clearly delineated stages and positions, while others have no such sequence of positions—each adopts only one aspect of the meaning without exhausting its source and flow.
Now, although there is no fixed position and no differentiation, this does not obstruct the distinctions of positions; briefly, there are two gates:
first, sequential arrangement (*xingbu*), and second, perfect fusion (*yuanrong*). These two support one another and are mutually unobstructed.
As for the dissemination of these words and deeds, the sequence and stages are clearly delineated; thus, while traversing the four heavens, six distinct positions are set forth.

In the second assembly, within the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the ten faiths are cultivated in conjunction with the manifestation of the ten profound depths. In the third assembly, at the Tuṣita Heaven palace, the ten abidings are finally expounded. In the fourth assembly, within the Yāma Heaven, the dharma-gate of the ten practices is revealed. In the fifth, at the Tuṣita Heaven, the ten transferences are taught. In the sixth, within the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the dharma-gate of the ten grounds is expounded. In the seventh, at the Hall of Universal Radiance, the two awakenings of Equality and Subtlety are correctly explained. In the eighth assembly, the perfect interfusion is correctly manifested.

Regarding the "ten faiths," they are: first, the mind of faith; second, the mind of diligence; third, the mind of mindfulness; fourth, the mind of concentration; fifth, the mind of wisdom; sixth, the mind of precepts; seventh, the mind of non-retrogression; eighth, the mind of protecting the Dharma; ninth, the mind of aspiration; and tenth, the mind of dedication.

Although these ten minds are complete, the successive stages have not yet been established; thus, no hierarchical distinctions are set forth. Rather, the ten kinds of profundity are manifested to reveal the practice and vows that accord with conditions. As previously explained, their virtuous functions encompass the beginning and the end.

Regarding the ten abodes: first, the abode of generating the mind; second, the abode of purifying the ground; third, the abode of cultivation; fourth, the abode of noble birth; fifth, the abode of perfecting skillful means; sixth, the abode of the correct mind; seventh, the abode of non-retrogression; eighth, the abode of youthful truth; ninth, the abode of the Dharma prince; and tenth, the abode of consecration.

The extensive and profound meaning of the text is fully contained within this assembly. Regarding the "ten practices" (*daśa-caryā*): first, the practice of joy; second, the practice of benefiting others;

third, the practice of non-opposition; fourth, the practice of being unbending; fifth, the practice of freedom from delusion and confusion; sixth, the practice of excellent manifestation; seventh, the practice of non-attachment; eighth, the practice that is difficult to attain; ninth, the practice of wholesome dharmas; and tenth, the practice of reality. These correspond, respectively, to the practices of giving (*dāna*) and so forth.
Although the Dharma-gate of the Ten Perfections (*daśapāramitā*) encompasses many aspects, the Ten Perfections are its primary focus.

As for the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), they are: first, the dedication of rescuing and protecting sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of sentient beings; second, the indestructible dedication; third, the dedication equal to all Buddhas; fourth, the dedication reaching all places; fifth, the dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit; sixth, the dedication that accords with and consolidates all roots of goodness; seventh, the dedication that equally accords with all sentient beings; eighth, the dedication of the mark of *tathatā* (suchness); ninth, the dedication of liberation without bondage or attachment; and tenth, the immeasurable dedication entering the *dharmadhātu*.
Within each stage, one fully cultivates all the perfections as the basis for dedication; each dedication is directed toward three points:
first, dedication to unsurpassed enlightenment; second, dedication to all sentient beings; and third, dedication to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of suchness.
The first two constitute dedication with signs (*sanimitta-pariṇāmanā*), while the last one constitutes dedication free from signs (*animitta-pariṇāmanā*).

When following and transcending signs are non-dual, and when phenomena and principle are cultivated in equal measure, such that compassion and wisdom are practiced in tandem, one will then be able to personally realize and enter [this state].

Regarding the ten stages (*bhūmi*): first, the Stage of Joy; second, the Stage of Purity; third, the Stage of Radiance; fourth, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom; fifth, the Stage of Difficult Victory; sixth, the Stage of Presence; seventh, the Stage of Far-Going; eighth, the Immovable Stage; ninth, the Stage of Excellent Wisdom; and tenth, the Stage of the Dharma Cloud.

However, these ten stages (bhūmis) are divided into ten because they involve the cultivation of ten superior practices, the severance of ten kinds of obstacles, and the realization of ten aspects of True Suchness (tathatā).
Each stage possesses four paths: first, the path of skillful means;

second, the path of realization; third, the path of assistance; and fourth, the path of non-abiding. This means that cultivating preparatory practices constitutes the path of skillful means; the direct realization of True Suchness constitutes the path of realization; the concurrent cultivation of various practices constitutes the path of assistance; and flowing simultaneously through both the provisional and the ultimate, without dwelling in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, constitutes the path of non-abiding.
Regarding the statement that the seventh assembly clarifies the two types of awakening—equal awakening (*samyaksambodhi*) and sublime awakening (*vibuddha*)—there are eleven chapters of scripture.

The first six chapters clarify the stage of equal awakening: namely, (1) the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis," (2) the "Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers," (3) the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences," (4) the "Chapter on the Incalculable," (5) the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Lifespan," and (6) the "Chapter on the Abodes of Bodhisattvas."

Regarding the term "Equal Enlightenment" (Samyaksambuddha): having already transcended the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and being equal to Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), one is called a Tathāgata by way of equality with Wondrous Enlightenment; yet, although equal, while still practicing, one is also called a Bodhisattva—the extensive characteristics of which are revealed in the sutras.
Regarding the term "Wondrous Enlightenment," there are five chapters of the sutra:
first, the "Chapter on the Buddha’s Inconceivable Dharmas," which generally elucidates the Buddha's virtues;
second, the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies," which specifically manifests the great marks.
Third, the "Chapter on the Merits of the Minor Marks and Radiance" specifically elucidates the minor marks;
fourth, the "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra" generally reveals the cessation of the perfect cause;

The first section distinguished the sequential arrangement (*saṃbhāra*), wherein the preceding and succeeding stages differ in depth and are not intermingled.

Second, to clarify the principle of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*): by means of the nature (*xing*) fusing with phenomena (*xiang*), a single stage encompasses all stages; whether the beginning subsumes the end, the end subsumes the beginning, the beginning and end subsume the middle, or the middle subsumes the beginning and end, the forty-two stages constitute the meaning of forty layers of mutual inclusion. Thus, while the eighth assembly contains the practices explained across all six stages, it omits their specific names to suddenly manifest all practices. Consequently, it is permitted that those at the initial stage of mind may achieve sudden awakening and also practice suddenly. Therefore, Bodhisattva Puhui (Samantabhadra) posed two hundred questions, and Bodhisattva Puxian (Samantabhadra) provided two thousand answers as the "two thousand practices," each one perfectly encompassing the whole.
This means that following any single practice subsumes two thousand practices; this is true for every practice, and thus they are perfectly interfused (*yuanrong*).
Although the sequential arrangement (*xingbu*) and the perfect interfusion are spoken of as having a temporal sequence, their meaning is actually simultaneous.
If one does not pass through the four heavens in succession, there is no way to manifest the sequential unfolding [of the teachings];
if they were not taught all at once in a single assembly, how could their perfect integration be revealed?

Sequential unfolding is the provisional arrangement of the teaching's form, while perfect integration is the functional virtue of the rational essence; since form is the manifestation of essence, sequential unfolding does not obstruct perfect integration.
The nature is the nature of phenomena; therefore, perfect interfusion does not obstruct sequential manifestation.
Because perfect interfusion does not obstruct sequential manifestation, the one becomes the immeasurable.
Because sequential manifestation does not obstruct perfect interfusion, the immeasurable becomes the one.

When the immeasurable becomes one, they interpenetrate in profound harmony; when the one becomes the immeasurable, they enter into one another in infinite layers. Thus, this can only be known by wisdom and is difficult for ordinary sentiments to fathom.

Fifteenth, the Ten Pāramitās.
Question:
Question: Among the various sūtras, the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) are frequently taught; why is it that ten are mentioned here?
Answer:
To ascend to the sublime station, one cannot do so without practice, yet although there are a thousand gateways of practice, they do not exceed these ten perfections.

The gateway of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) is taught to remedy the six defects; however, because one wishes to manifest their perfect fusion and further remedy ten obstacles, the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) are taught.
Nevertheless, each and every perfection encompasses all others; they are categorized as ten types according to the predominance or subordination of their respective qualities:

first, giving (*dāna*); second, ethical discipline (*śīla*); third, patience (*kṣānti*); fourth, diligence (*vīrya*); fifth, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); sixth, wisdom (*prajñā*); seventh, skillful means (*upāya*); eighth, aspiration (*praṇidhāna*); ninth, power (*bala*); and tenth, knowledge (*jñāna*).
Generosity consists of giving material goods, the Dharma, and fearlessness, such that there is nothing not relinquished;
ethical discipline prevents what is wrong and ceases evil, remaining flawless both internally and externally;
patience involves remaining unperturbed by either favorable or adverse conditions, and through discernment, accepting them with composure.
Through diligence, one leaves behind the characteristics of body and mind, and the myriad practices are cultivated and increased;
through meditative concentration, thought and deliberation both vanish, and the mind rests peacefully within the realm of reality;
through wisdom, the mind is free from discrimination, and one skillfully realizes the emptiness of nature.
Regarding skillful means (*upāya*), one engages with existence while remaining constantly in emptiness, such that all actions are unimpeded;
regarding vows (*praṇidhāna*), one seeks the higher while transforming those below, extending to the very end of the future;
regarding the power of strength (*bala*), the merits of reflection and cultivation are perfected, such that one is unmoved by the myriad objects of perception.

The Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā) brings decisive resolution free from delusion and realizes the Dharma to gladden the spirit. Sometimes, within a single thought-moment, all ten perfections arise simultaneously;

thus the Sūtra says: "One practices giving without grasping at signs; one fundamentally cuts off all evils while firmly upholding the precepts; one understands that phenomena are harmless and remains ever patient; one knows the nature of phenomena is detached and is always diligent; having exhausted all afflictions, one enters the various dhyānas; one skillfully masters the emptiness of nature and discerns all dharmas; being fully endowed with the power of wisdom, one is able to provide universal salvation; by extinguishing all evils, one is called a Great Being (Mahāsattva)."
The extensive meaning of the ten perfections is fully contained in the *Great Commentary* (Dàshū).
This is my respectful response.
Sixteenth: The reason for teaching the ten.
Question:

Within the various sūtras, the characteristics of dharmas follow their respective meanings; as for the three bodies, four wisdoms, five eyes, and six supernormal powers, they vary according to whether their number is reduced or increased, and thus cannot be standardized.
Question: Why does this teaching frequently speak of ten?
Answer:
The truth is perfectly interfused and is not manifested apart from its forms; because one wishes to reveal its perfect subtlety, it relies upon the number ten to clarify it.
Ten is the number of a complete cycle because it represents a circle; if there were more, it would be difficult to exhaustively describe, and if there were fewer, it would not manifest completeness.

Furthermore, speaking according to the ultimate principle, the ten directions are fully present. Thus, the five eyes are expanded into the ten eyes, and the three bodies are fully explained as the ten bodies. This is intended so that everything encountered may be perfectly integrated, with each and every thing entering the Dharma-realm; therefore, it can be understood that the number ten is frequently used.

Seventeenth: Immediate Transcendence from Hell.
Question:
Sins have degrees of depth and rank has its gradations; how could an evildoer of the most heinous crimes in the Avīci Hell suddenly leap over all these stages to ascend directly to the Ten Grounds?
If you claim it was through the power of the sutra or the radiance of the Buddha, why did they not discourse on the sutras while still within the hell?
Why rely upon the light of constant illumination?
I look up to set forth the reason for this in order to dispel great doubts.
Answer:

The ocean of the Perfect Teaching’s profound function is inconceivable; though the Buddhas’ majestic spiritual power brings benefit and joy beyond measure, its transformation of beings necessarily depends upon the presence of karmic affinity.

When those in the hells who heard the Perfect Dharma in the past—possessing the adamantine seed—encounter the Buddha’s light, the moment that light flows to them and they attain the Way is precisely when their faculties and capacities have reached maturity.

The profound mechanism of striking the Sage results in a mutual resonance between the Way and its response; this is like a sprout long imbued with yang energy that suddenly sends forth shoots when brushed by an easterly breeze.

Although the state may be realized instantaneously, the cause was accumulated through goodness; had it not been for such a vessel, one would not have encountered the light. Through gradual cultivation over time, the fruit is attained without suddenness.
That shadows follow forms and echoes pursue sounds is a matter of natural principle; how could it cause any confusion?
This is my respectful reply.
Eighteenth: The Deafness and Blindness of the Two Vehicles.
Question:
If even those in the most wretched hells encounter the Buddha’s light, why are the noble stream-enterers among the śrāvakas so suddenly deaf and blind?

Furthermore, in the *Lotus Sūtra*, they were cleared from their seats and sent away so that they could not hear [the teaching], yet Puṇyaraśmi caused them to hear it and thereby obtained long-lasting benefit.
How is it that this scripture alone differs from other sutras?
Please explain its origins so as to clear away the web of doubt.
Answer:

Through many avenues of causes and conditions, he teaches and transforms the myriad classes of beings; their faculties vary in magnitude, and the benefit they receive varies in depth. Those in the hells who possess the perfect seed attain benefit that transcends all at once. Yet those of the Two Vehicles, lacking the requisite capacity, do not perceive him even when facing him—just as thunder shaking the earth is not heard by the deaf, and the sun and moon shining in the sky are not seen by the blind. This principle is so manifest; how could one be deluded about it?

Furthermore, the ritual principles of the Great Sage’s transformation are not uniform. In the *Lotus Sūtra*, he commands with awe to exhort those within the assembly; by having the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging make his presence known, there is a distant benefit. The various śrāvakas neither slander nor practice [the teaching], and their failure to hear it is preserved to manifest their severed lot, thereby revealing that the Dharma is perfectly wondrous and not shared with the two vehicles.
Each has its own specific aim, yet their meanings do not deviate from one another.

Nineteenth: The Vows of Samantabhadra’s Conduct.
Question:
Both this sutra and other sutras speak of the practices and vows of Samantabhadra; which of these is it?
Please provide a detailed analysis.
Answer:

The teaching of the One Vehicle was first illuminated upon the high mountain; the wondrous causes of the ten bodies must rely upon great practice. These practices all accord with principle and are universally pervasive; within a single practice, all practices are subsumed, and the entire ocean of all practices is fully contained within a single speck of dust.
When the myriad practices boil over and the single path is truly good, its very substance may already be called the conduct of Samantabhadra.
This universal conduct is that which Samantabhadra practices; furthermore, by means of this conduct, one also becomes Samantabhadra.

The names "person" (pudgala) and "dharma" are both established through mutual dependence; they distinguish this from the sequential, distributed practices [of the śrāvakas]. Because his virtue pervades the entire dharma-realm, he is called "Universal" (Samantabhadra); because he is supremely compliant, harmonious, and virtuous, he is called "Worthy" (Bhadra).
Briefly summarized, ten gates are presented to reveal its inexhaustibility:
first, the universality of that which is sought, because one must seek the equal realization of all Tathāgatas;
second, the universality of those to be transformed, because one must transform the inexhaustible realm of sentient beings.
Third is the universality of what is to be abandoned, because one must sever the boundless ocean of afflictions.
Fourth is the universality of the practice of activities, because there is not a single activity that is not performed.
Fifth is the universality of the practice of principle, because each and every practice of activity penetrates the source of nature.
Sixth is the universality of unimpeded practice, because the two practices of phenomena and principle mutually penetrate one another.
Seventh is the universality of integrated practice, because each and every single practice encompasses the inexhaustible.
Eighth, the universality of the arising of activity, because there is no place where its activity does not pervade.
Ninth, the universality of the sphere of practice, because the aforementioned eight gates extend throughout all places within the Indra-net of lands.
The tenth [perfection] is that of universal practice, because throughout the three periods of time, the integration of eons and moments is boundless and without end.

These ten aforementioned practices are interwoven yet unmixed, constituting the conduct of Samantabhadra; though scattered throughout various sutras, they are fully present in this fundamental teaching.

Twenty: The Patriarch Mañjuśrī.
Question:
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva manifests as a person of the causal stage; how then can he be called the "Mother of Buddhas"?
Since he is a Dharma-body Bodhisattva, why does he dwell specifically at Qingliang?

Some say he received the teachings directly from Śākyamuni, while others say he came from the Golden Land; some call him the ancestor of all Buddhas, while others describe him as the teacher of Bodhisattvas. By tracing back to the source and following the current to clarify his standard and measure, those who investigate the profound mystery shall not be confused by what they see and hear.
Answer:
The Most Holy and Most Divine One is difficult to fathom in His fundamental nature; relying upon the teachings and the principles, I shall briefly recount what has been seen and heard.

He manifested traces through human beings, yet has long since attained perfect enlightenment; His essence pervades the Dharma-realm, and thus His responsive manifestations must necessarily have their proper methods.

The gate of attaining the fruit without abandoning the cause: though his present traces are those of a disciple of Śākyamuni, in the past he was the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light (Prabhāsa), serving as the ancestral teacher for nine generations; how much more so, since there is none who has not followed him in generating the aspiration for enlightenment—he is thus the progenitor of all Buddhas.

It primarily emphasizes the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, which is further known as the Mother of Buddhas; relying upon the true source of immovability, it speaks from the Golden World. When people of Zhendan experienced a resonance with it, it came to reside specifically on Mount Qingliang.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* briefly states its origin as the Tathāgata Dragon-Species Supreme Honored King;
the *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* speaks of his manifestation in the present as Maṇiratnasañcaya.

The *Womb Sūtra* (*Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*) states that throughout the ten directions all have realized bodhi; their number exceeds that of the sands of the Ganges, such that even the sages cannot calculate it. They manifest transformations identical to the myriad species and enter the dust-motes of the Indra-net worlds; yet within the true source of profound, singular stillness, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
The mouth desires to speak, yet words fail; the mind intends to follow after objects, yet thoughts cease.
Formlessness manifests as form, and the cool clarity appears in manifold ways;
the body is itself bodiless, for the golden countenance shines before the eyes yet cannot be seen.

Those who cling to appearances are deluded regarding the ultimate goal; those who contemplate emptiness are confused by what they see and hear. Those confused by what they see and hear seek emptiness exclusively outside of existence, while those deluded regarding the ultimate goal mistake the moon reflected in water for a precious gem. Thus, people of middling capacity may delight in the elephant [metaphor] yet remain stuck in two paths, while those of inferior capacity disregard empty appearances as mere strange anomalies.
How could such strange and supernatural phenomena arise only momentarily at dawn and dusk, when they are the constant reality for a thousand autumns and ten thousand years?

Moreover, since the Venerable Xuan received his mandate from the various heavens and the divine monks manifested their glory within this sacred realm—receiving offerings from the eight provinces of the High Qi dynasty and receiving the returned radiance of the ten emperors of the Tang—the fact that Qingliang is a holy abode is beyond doubt. Since the True Source is omnipresent, what cause is there for further suspicion?
I hope to look up to their sagely spirit, without being able to fathom its depth or shallowness.

Twenty-first: The Simultaneous Flow of Compassion and Wisdom.
Question:
Since profound Prajñā-pāramitā directly reaches the source of the mind, why is it necessary to involve oneself in the flux of worldly affairs through compassion?
Answer:
The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma essentially consists of these two:

wisdom that realizes the true realm and compassion that brings universal salvation. If one has compassion but lacks wisdom, one is bound by attachment and views; if one has wisdom but lacks compassion, one falls to the level of the Two Vehicles.

Now, employing the wisdom that forgets artifice to guide compassion that has no fixed object, one does not linger in the two extremes of emptiness and existence, nor dwell in either nirvana or samsara; thus, while engaging with the phenomenal world to transform sentient beings, one never loses sight of emptiness, and while contemplating quiescent extinction with a mind free of conceptualization, one continues to transform the four types of birth and the nine classes of beings.
Just as two wheels enable one to travel far, when compassion and wisdom are both complete, the fruit is perfected.

Twenty-second: The Conjoined Practice of Śamatha and Vipaśyanā.

Within the Buddha-dharma, wisdom is the foremost; one should cultivate only wisdom, for all six perfections and myriad practices lead to the realization of bodhi.
Why, then, do the sutras specifically emphasize meditative concentration and wisdom, or speak of them as being practiced together?

Although wisdom is honored, its illumination is not profound without concentration.

Without wisdom, meditation cannot exhaust its stillness; without meditation, wisdom cannot deepen its illumination. Therefore, only when stillness and wisdom flow together can the fruit of Buddhahood be realized.

Twenty-third: Mastery over Movement and Stillness.
Question:
When one accords with the principle of stillness such that both the internal and external are merged in obscurity, how can one perform actions and further give rise to great function?
Answer:
Śrāvakas seek the truth outside of quiescence and phenomena; thus, their movement is not quiescence.

Bodhisattvas embody principle within phenomena such that they are true even amidst activity; though they move, they are without movement and do not obstruct constant quiescence. Therefore, they manifest dignified deportment without arising from the samādhi of cessation.

Twenty-fourth: The Integration of Phenomena and Principle.
Question:
While phenomena differ in ten thousand ways, their principle is of a single flavor. How then can the sutras say that phenomena and principle are unimpeded and mutually identical?
Answer:
To seek the principle apart from phenomena is the partial truth of the Two Vehicles; to realize that phenomena are themselves the principle is the great awakening of the Bodhisattvas.
Outside of form there is no emptiness; the entirety of form is emptiness. Outside of emptiness there is no form; the entirety of emptiness is form.
Form refers to phenomena produced through conditions; emptiness refers to the principle of the absence of intrinsic nature.
Because they arise through conditions, that which lacks intrinsic nature is the very reality of form, yet it is true emptiness;
because they lack intrinsic nature, that which arises from conditions is the very principle of emptiness, yet it functions as the reality of form.
The single essence and two meanings are designated as "phenomenon" (shi) and "principle" (li); because these two meanings constitute a single essence, they are able to interpenetrate one another.

Twenty-fifth, manifesting the Ten Mysteries.
Question:
I have heard that the profound meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra is termed the "Ten Mysteries. Please list their names and briefly explain their significance.
Answer:
The ten [aspects] manifest inexhaustibly, each one creating the profound mystery; as soon as a single dharma is raised, it is complete with these ten.
The first is called the Gate of Simultaneous Mutual Fulfillment and Correspondence, like a single drop of seawater containing the flavors of a hundred rivers.
Second is the gate of the unimpeded mastery over breadth and narrowness, like a mirror only a foot wide that reflects images from a thousand li away.
Third is the gate of the mutual containment of the one and the many without confusion, like a thousand lamps in a single room whose lights interpenetrate one another.
Fourth is the gate of the mutual sovereignty of the characteristics of all phenomena, like gold and its golden color, which are inseparable from one another.
Fifth is the gate of the simultaneous accomplishment of the hidden and the manifest through secrecy, like a crescent moon in a clear sky, where darkness and light coexist.
Sixth is the gate of the subtle containment and establishment of mutual compatibility, like a crystal vase filled with many mustard seeds.
Seventh is the gate of the realm of Indra’s net, like two mirrors reflecting each other, transmitting light and mirroring one another so that they emerge in an endless succession.
8. The Gate of Manifesting the Dharma by Relying on Phenomena to Generate Understanding: as when an image is established and the arm is raised, everything encountered by the eye becomes the Way.
9. The Gate of Accomplishing through the Separation of Worlds and the Difference of Dharmas: as in a single night’s dream where one soars for a hundred years.
The tenth is the Gate of the Perfect Clarity and Endowment of Principal and Retinue, like the North Star around which all the stars revolve in unison.
These ten aspects are without sequence; by mentioning one, the whole is fully encompassed. This constitutes the unique, profound principle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
